**BIRMINGHAM, Alabama (CNN) —** If Russell Jackson has his way, every child who needs medical care but lacks transportation will have a safe, reliable way to get there.

Jackson founded Kid One, an organization that has transported thousands of children to medical appointments.

“We found that there were more than 80,000 children in Alabama living in homes without a car,” Jackson says. “And in rural areas, there are no cabs, no buses, no trains. ... Millions of children across our country lack access to medical care every day because they have no way to reach it.”

So determined was Jackson to address the problem that, in 1997, he left his career as an Alabama firefighter, moved in with friends and tapped into his retirement account to establish Kid One Transport, a nonprofit organization that provides transportation for children in need throughout his home state.

Over 11 years, Kid One’s fleet of vans transported more than 16,000 children to and from scheduled medical appointments across Alabama.

*Watch Jackson describe the need for medical transportation in rural Alabama »*

Jackson never expected to leave the fire department to lead a nonprofit organization. After all, firefighting had been the fulfillment of a lifelong dream.

“What little boy doesn’t want to be a firefighter?” Jackson says with a laugh.

But an emergency call to his department in March 1992 changed everything. Jackson was dispatched to assist an unresponsive 2-year-old who had accidentally hanged himself in the family car while trying to retrieve a toy.

“We did everything we could to try to revive that young child,” he says.

Despite their efforts, the 2-year-old died.

“I took it pretty hard,” Jackson recalls. “It’s not that I hadn’t been exposed to tragedies before, but this one affected me differently.”

On the advice of a counselor, Jackson began volunteering to help process his grief. A friend suggested that he volunteer in the small rural town of Sayre, Alabama. Jackson was stunned by what he found just 25 minutes from his home.

“When I drove into the community, it was a world of its own. Many of the homes were deplorable, and that’s really the only way I can describe them,” he says.

Jackson says he immediately felt ashamed of his own comfortable lifestyle.

*Watch Jackson describe the “turning point” that led to Kid One Transport »*

“All it took was that one visit,” he recalls, “and I knew I wanted to come out and work hand in hand with these people, doing whatever I could to make life a little easier for them.”

When social workers told him about neighborhood children who had no way to travel to and from appointments for chemotherapy, physical therapy or even routine checkups, Jackson began driving them himself.

Before long, the one-man operation had grown into a 13-van team serving 30 counties.

Although Jackson recently stepped away from a day-to-day role in the organization he founded, he says the most rewarding part of his work has been meeting the families and witnessing firsthand so many medical transformations. Some children learned to speak, another learned to walk, and others recovered from life-threatening illnesses—even when doctors had little hope.

*Watch a child who relies on Kid One to get to medical appointments »*

“I saw so many lives changed—so many determined children and parents who wanted to overcome the odds against them,” Jackson says.

He believes that helping them reach the care they needed made all the difference.

“We’re the missing piece of the puzzle that prevents so many people from accessing what we would consider world-class medicine. ... To know that they overcame it all because of a simple ride,” he adds, “has made founding Kid One Transport worth every bit of effort.”

# Former firefighter turns a ride to the doctor into a lifeline for Alabama children

**By CNN**

For many families, getting a sick child to the doctor means rearranging a work schedule, buckling into the car and navigating traffic.

For others, the absence of a reliable vehicle can turn a routine appointment into an impossible journey.

Russell Jackson saw that problem up close while working as an Alabama firefighter. Children were missing medical appointments not because their parents did not care, but because they had no dependable way to get there.

So Jackson set out to provide one.

He founded Kid One Transport, a nonprofit that offers free transportation to medical appointments for children and expectant mothers in need. Its vehicles have become a bridge between families and the health care that may otherwise remain out of reach.

The idea was straightforward: If transportation was the barrier, remove it.

But the service has always been about more than a ride. For parents already juggling medical concerns, limited incomes, jobs and other children, transportation can carry hidden costs. A long-distance appointment may require fuel money they do not have. Public transit may be unavailable, especially in rural communities. Friends and relatives may not be able to help repeatedly.

Missing an appointment can delay a diagnosis, interrupt treatment or allow a manageable condition to become an emergency.

Jackson understood emergencies. Firefighters are trained to respond when a crisis is already underway. With Kid One Transport, he found a way to intervene earlier — before a missed checkup or treatment created a more serious problem.

The organization coordinates trips for children who need access to pediatricians, specialists, therapy and other medical services. Some rides are short. Others require traveling from smaller Alabama communities to medical centers in larger cities.

Each trip represents a family that does not have to choose between health care and transportation.

Jackson’s work also highlights an often-overlooked part of the American health care system. A doctor may be available. A treatment may exist. An appointment may even be scheduled. But none of that matters if the patient cannot reach the clinic.

Transportation is considered a social determinant of health, one of the everyday circumstances that can shape whether people receive care and how healthy they are. The problem can be especially acute for children, who depend on adults not only to arrange care but also to get them there.

Kid One Transport was built around that gap.

Jackson brought to the mission the service-minded instincts of a first responder: identify the need, show up and help. Instead of a fire engine, the response came in the form of a vehicle arriving at a family’s home.

The result is a quieter kind of rescue — one measured in appointments kept, treatments continued and worries eased.

For the families Kid One Transport serves, the journey may end at a hospital or doctor’s office. But Jackson’s larger destination has always been access: making sure a child’s chance to get well is not determined by whether there is a car in the driveway.

# Kid One Transport Turns Firefighter’s Concern Into Lifeline for Alabama Children

**BIRMINGHAM, Ala.** — Russell Jackson created Kid One Transport after seeing how a lack of reliable transportation could turn a manageable health problem into an emergency for Alabama children.

While working as a firefighter and paramedic, Jackson encountered families who relied on emergency services because they had no way to reach routine medical appointments. Children were missing checkups and treatments, allowing illnesses to worsen until parents had little choice but to call 911 or seek emergency care.

That experience convinced Jackson that transportation was an essential part of health care. He founded Kid One Transport in 1997 to provide free rides to medical appointments for children and expectant mothers who otherwise might not be able to get there.

Jackson’s firefighting background helped shape the nonprofit’s preventive mission. Rather than waiting for a medical crisis, Kid One aims to help families reach pediatricians, specialists, dentists, therapy providers and prenatal-care appointments before conditions become emergencies.

Operating across Alabama, the nonprofit coordinates transportation for low-income and medically vulnerable families, including those who must travel long distances for specialized treatment.

Since its creation, Kid One Transport says it has provided **more than 400,000 free medical trips for Alabama children and expectant mothers**. The figure represents rides rather than a count of unique patients, but it reflects the broad reach of Jackson’s original idea: that something as simple as a safe ride can protect a child’s health and, in some cases, save a life.

# The Long Road to a Doctor: How Transportation Barriers Keep Rural Alabama Children from Care

For many Alabama families, getting a child to the doctor is not simply a matter of making an appointment. It can require finding a working car, buying enough gasoline for a long trip, taking unpaid time off work and arranging care for other children. In communities without public transportation—and where pediatric specialists may be hours away—those obstacles can make healthcare effectively unreachable.

Russell Jackson, founder of Kid One Transport, has spent years confronting that problem. The Alabama nonprofit provides free transportation to medical care for children and expectant mothers who otherwise may have no reliable way to reach appointments. Its work illustrates a basic but often overlooked truth: Healthcare does little good when patients cannot get to it.

## Distance becomes a medical risk

Rural Alabama residents commonly travel outside their counties for specialized treatment. A child may receive routine care nearby but need to go to Birmingham, Huntsville, Montgomery or Mobile for cardiology, oncology, neurology, surgery or other specialized services.

That distance creates a chain of potential barriers. Many low-income households have one vehicle—or none. A shared car may be needed by an adult who cannot miss work without losing wages or risking a job. Older vehicles may not be dependable enough for a lengthy highway trip. Even when a family has transportation, gasoline, parking and meals on the road add costs that may be difficult to absorb.

The consequences extend beyond a missed appointment. Delayed care can allow manageable conditions to worsen. Children may miss follow-up visits, diagnostic tests, therapy sessions or medication checks. Chronic illnesses such as asthma, diabetes and seizure disorders often require consistent monitoring, while treatments for cancer and other serious conditions may depend on a strict schedule.

A transportation problem can therefore become a health crisis.

## Kid One Transport fills a critical gap

Jackson created Kid One Transport around the idea that no child should miss necessary medical care because the family lacks a ride. The organization coordinates no-cost trips for eligible families, using drivers and vehicles to connect patients with hospitals, clinics and specialists.

The service is more complicated than taking someone across town. Rural pickups can require a driver to travel a substantial distance before the child’s trip even begins. A single appointment may consume most of a day once pickup time, travel, waiting and the return journey are included.

Children may also need car seats, wheelchair accommodations or space for medical equipment. Some must travel repeatedly for therapy or treatment. Others need to reach an early-morning procedure, when informal options such as asking a friend or relative may not be available.

By organizing transportation around medical needs, Kid One Transport provides something that ordinary transit systems and ride-hailing services often cannot: dependable, child-focused travel over long distances at no cost to the family.

Jackson’s work also exposes how transportation affects the entire healthcare system. When a child misses an appointment, a clinic loses time that could have been used for another patient. When preventive or follow-up care is delayed, the child may later need more intensive—and more expensive—treatment. A ride can help preserve continuity of care while reducing the risk that a manageable problem ends in an emergency room.

## Rural conditions magnify the problem

Transportation barriers exist in cities, but rural geography makes them more severe. Alabama has many communities with little or no fixed-route public transit. Taxis and app-based ride services may be scarce, expensive or unavailable, especially for families traveling across county lines.

At the same time, healthcare services have become more concentrated. Rural hospital instability and the loss of some local obstetric and specialty services have forced patients to travel farther. Pregnant women may need transportation for prenatal visits and delivery-related care, while children born with complicated medical needs may require repeated trips to major pediatric centers.

Formal transportation benefits, including non-emergency medical transportation available through Medicaid, can help some families. But such programs do not eliminate every difficulty. Families may struggle with scheduling, eligibility rules, advance-notice requirements or trips that involve long waits and multiple appointments. Children whose households do not qualify may still lack a safe, reliable vehicle.

Informal transportation is uncertain as well. A neighbor may be able to help once, but not every week. A parent may borrow a car, but not for a daylong journey. Rural families often piece together transportation until one part of the arrangement fails.

## Missed care has lasting effects

Children are especially vulnerable to delays because their development is time-sensitive. Missing hearing tests, speech therapy, physical therapy or behavioral-health appointments can affect performance in school and long-term well-being. Delayed dental care can turn a cavity into an infection. Gaps in prenatal care can endanger both a mother and her baby.

The burden also falls unevenly. Families with higher incomes can pay for repairs, rental cars, hotels or private transportation. Low-income families must often choose among necessities: gasoline, food, utilities and medicine. For them, distance is not merely inconvenient; it is a financial barrier.

These challenges can be easy for policymakers to underestimate because transportation is frequently treated as separate from healthcare. Yet for the families served by Jackson and Kid One Transport, the two are inseparable. A specialist may be available and an appointment may be scheduled, but without a safe ride, access exists only on paper.

## More than charity is needed

Organizations such as Kid One Transport provide an essential safety net, but nonprofits alone cannot solve a statewide infrastructure problem. Alabama’s response could include stronger rural transit networks, better coordination among healthcare providers and transportation programs, expanded support for non-emergency medical travel, and more investment in local clinics and telehealth.

Hospitals can also screen patients for transportation insecurity when appointments are made, rather than waiting until a child repeatedly misses care. Scheduling multiple visits on the same day, offering flexible appointment times and connecting families quickly with transportation providers can reduce unnecessary trips.

Telehealth can help with some follow-up care, but it is not a complete substitute. Families may lack broadband access, and many examinations, tests and treatments must be performed in person.

Russell Jackson and Kid One Transport demonstrate what becomes possible when transportation is treated as part of healthcare rather than an afterthought. Every completed trip represents more than miles traveled. It means a child receives a test, sees a specialist or continues treatment on schedule.

In rural Alabama, the road to better health can be long. For many children, the first and most important form of medical assistance is simply a reliable way to get there.
